sample.summary: PGIM argues that commodities deserve a strategic, dynamic place in multi-asset portfolios rather than being treated as a tactical add-on, citing a macro regime of more frequent shocks, supply constraints that slow the response to price rises, and the diversification value of assets driven by physical supply and demand rather than discount rates or earnings. It notes that commodities have historically performed well during high-inflation periods, when equities and Treasuries delivered returns close to zero in real terms, while lagging during low-inflation periods, so allocation size should reflect the intended role, risk budget and cyclicality. PGIM stresses that commodity strategies vary widely in benchmark design, net exposure, signal breadth and risk controls, and that allocators should judge them on economic rationale, signal robustness across regimes, risk distribution and implementation quality.

tags.call_text: Commodities merit a strategic, dynamic allocation in multi-asset portfolios.

sample.title: Myron Scholes on Time: The total portfolio approach and dynamic risk management
sample.summary: Janus Henderson Investors argues that the total portfolio approach, which still relies on a static reference portfolio that lets fund risk drift with markets, should evolve to start from a drawdown budget and manage total risk to it daily. It contends that dynamic risk budget utilisation (taking more risk when opportunities are rich, less when they are not, and knowing when to re-risk after losses) and planning for shocks so that long-horizon funds can supply liquidity rather than be forced sellers should lift compound returns, which it describes as a fund's "North Star". The firm's explicit view is that this requires quantitative talent, a crisis playbook and a CIO who builds trust with the board.

tags.call_text: Total portfolio approach should start from a drawdown budget and manage risk dynamically.

sample.title: Make smart decisions about your time with the Time-Value Equation
sample.summary: Fidelity Investments argues that advisors' "lack of time," which they cite as their top barrier to growth, can be addressed by treating time as a resource to be managed deliberately, using its Time-Value Equation framework. The framework focuses on three levers: who advisors spend time with (segmenting clients by asset level and planning complexity to simplify services for high-impact relationships), what they focus on in client engagements (moving up the Advice Value Stack by understanding clients' broader financial and personal goals), and how they allocate time (adopting technology, outsourcing, or delegating lower-value tasks). Fidelity's explicit call is for advisors and firm leaders to become "stewards of time," reinvesting freed capacity in organic growth and deeper client relationships, while the piece promotes its own tools and model portfolio and asset allocation solutions as enablers.
